text:
Philip Rubin is a prominent researcher and leader in the fields of computational, linguistic, and cognitive science. He earned a Bachelor of Arts in psychology and linguistics from Brandeis University and a PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut under the supervision of Michael Turvey, Ignatius Mattingly, Philip Lieberman, and Alvin Liberman.
His research focuses on embodied cognition, particularly the biological bases of speech and language. He is best known for his pioneering work in articulatory synthesis, speech perception, and sinewave synthesis. Key contributions include the development of the ASY (Articulatory Synthesis) and SWS (Sinewave Synthesis) programs, which model the physiology and acoustics of speech production. He also developed the HADES signal processing system and the SPIEL programming language, a precursor to MATLAB.
Rubin has held significant leadership roles in science administration and policy, including serving as Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation (NSF) and as Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). He has been a strong advocate for science policy, human subjects research protections, and ethical considerations in emerging technologies.
He is a Fellow of the Acoustical Society of America, the American Psychological Association, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and the American Psychological Society. Rubin has received numerous awards, including the Distinguished Service Award from COSSA and the iGIANT Pioneer Award. He is also a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences (FABBS), where he currently serves as President.
Beyond his scientific work, Rubin is a photographer, co-founder of the IS Group, and has contributed to public science engagement through various initiatives. He is recognized for his interdisciplinary approach, combining computational modeling with physiological and psychological insights to advance understanding of human speech and cognition.
